inline.s: Having said this, he handed the blade to Changchun. Qiu Changchun took the knife in hand and was about to cut his own throat when suddenly he heard a voice in mid-air call out: “Qiu Changchun, return my court tablet (
hù

, the slender scepter held in the hand by ministers of old when attending court) to me!” Changchun looked up and saw three army officers standing within five-colored auspicious clouds, who said: “We three are the Three Officials of Heaven, Earth, and Water. Because we saw that your mind of the Way was firm and your ascetic practice complete, we have come especially to transform and liberate you. You have indeed given up yourself for others, accumulating merit and practicing good deeds. Now we will change your mortal body into a body of the Way, and turn your illusory frame into an immortal frame. Six years of awakening to the Way are accomplished, and seven years of becoming a true one are about to flourish. You may press forward diligently and not delay.”

Suddenly Changchun’s mind was luminously enlightened, and his spiritual faculty was made manifest. Looking again at what he held in his hand, it was a court tablet, not some steel knife. He also saw that among the Three Officials one had empty hands; knowing it was his court tablet, he could do nothing but ascend and return it. He tried leaping his body upward, and he was already within the clouds, presenting the tablet. The Three Officials, riding their colored clouds, gradually departed. Qiu Changchun was about to spring down from the clouds when he suddenly remembered the hempen-robed physiognomist, who had determined that he was destined to die of starvation. “My fruit of the Way is now accomplished,” he thought, “surely I cannot suffer hunger again. Why not take advantage of this cloud and go east of the river, to test him once more, and see how keen his eyesight is?”

His resolve being fixed, he immediately turned the cloud around. In an instant he had traveled a thousand li and arrived before the villa of Sai Mayi (the Hempen-Robed Contender). Descending from the clouds, he entered the villa. He saw a man in his twenties — the very lad who had brought out the rice that year — and said to him: “I have come to ask the old gentleman to read my face.” The man said: “My father has long not gone out. If you wish to have your countenance read, come with me to the hall.” Thereupon he led Changchun inside. Sai Mayi was seated in the hall, and seeing Changchun enter, he rose quickly to receive him, treating him with the courtesy due to a guest, and asked him to sit and drink tea.
Changchun saw that Sai Mayi’s beard and hair were all white, and that he was aged and doddering, so he said: “Several years have passed, and, sir, you have in an instant (
shū

, suddenly) grown hoary of hair and beard.” Sai Mayi said: “This old man does not know where he has met the Daoist master, and has for the moment forgotten.” Qiu Changchun said: “Does the gentleman not recall the ‘serpent locking the mouth’ — the man who was to die of starvation?” Hearing this, Sai Mayi examined his features, clapped his hands, and laughed aloud: “Wonderful! Wonderful! Where has the Daoist master gone to perform such great merit that he has changed the countenance of former years?” Qiu Changchun said: “The gentleman once said that physiognomy is fixed for life, and never changes; how is it that today you speak of a change?” The hempen-robed physiognomist said: “This old man only knows how to read the face, and not the heart. Today the master’s face has changed along with his heart — this is beyond this old man’s knowledge. Formerly the two lines entered the mouth, which is called the ‘serpent locking the mouth’ and portended death by starvation. Now these two lines have separated and go around the position of chengjiang. Upon this chengjiang there has also grown a small red mole, forming a pattern called ‘two dragons playing with a pearl.’ It is auspicious beyond words — it portends that you will receive the offerings of an emperor, and that your merit and fortune will be immeasurable. How could this foolish old man have known it?” Hearing this, Changchun also admired his supernatural skill in physiognomy, and took his leave.

He returned to the Panxi temple to sit in meditation. Only because he had stirred up a thought of calculation, going to mock Sai Mayi, he again drew upon himself a host of obstacles. As he was sitting in meditation, in a dazed state between existing and not existing, he seemed to be amid ten thousand mountains. Suddenly a wild wind arose, and a yellow-spotted fierce tiger appeared, baring its fangs and brandishing its claws, leaping at him. But he took this word ‘death’ lightly and paid it no heed at all. Again reaching a dark (
yǎo

), obscure, and dim point, he saw a young Daoist lad come and say: “My master Ma Danyang has arrived; why does the master not rise and meet him?” Sure enough, Danyang came from below. Changchun reflected: the Way does not cling to affection; whether he comes or goes, let him. Suddenly many people came and said: “It was hard for you to carry us across the river; now at the time of harvest we have gathered for you more than a stone of wheat, enough for the whole year’s food and use. We have also helped you with two strings of cash to sew a garment.” Having said this, they carried the wheat before him and piled it high, and brought the two strings of copper cash to his side, asking him to take them with his own hand, yet he was even less concerned. In his stupor he saw again a beautiful woman of seventeen or eighteen. She said she had been cruelly beaten by her stepmother and had run away in secret, wishing to go to her maternal uncle’s home; but being alone and helpless, she asked, “Old master, would you not escort me there? I shall be endlessly grateful.” Saying this, tender and alluring, she seemed about to weep and to plead. Changchun paid her no attention at all, giving her a state of no person and no self, neither knowing nor perceiving. In the twinkling of an eye, his second sister-in-law came with several children and told him: “Your second brother has died, and your elder uncle has swallowed up the family estate alone. He has left these your nephews and nieces without clothing to last them through life, nor food to last them through the day. I am but a woman; how can I raise them? For your second brother’s sake, and mindful of the bond of flesh and blood, how will you settle us mother and children?” Having said this, the children pulled and tugged at him, weeping and wailing, calling ‘third uncle’ long and ‘third uncle’ short, without ceasing, wanting food and wanting drink, grasping and clawing at him wildly. In the deepest stillness, wisdom suddenly arose in Changchun, as if there were nothing at all. Suddenly he heard a loud sound in mid-air; the South Heaven Gate opened wide, and he saw two lads leading a white crane before him, saying: “By the Jade Emperor’s decree (
chì
, the imperial edict and command of the sovereign), we invite the True Man to ride the crane and ascend.” And hear the next chapter for the outcome.
Let not the three common defilements breed illusory realms; beware lest the six thieves disturb the field of the mind.

blocks.text: 25. When True Yang Is Full, the Host of Yin Retreats and Scatters; When Evil Is Filled to the Brim, the Whole Family Sinks

inline.s: Below the northern suburbs the graves are ranged, amid tangled, blurring grass strange birds call;
Long lying in the grave-mound the man does not wake; peach withered and plum fallen, the Qingming festival passes.

The story goes that Qiu Changchun sat in meditation and applied his practice in the Panxi temple. While he was in a state of emptiness and stillness, he suddenly saw two lads leading a white crane before him, saying: “By the command of the Emperor of Heaven, we invite the True Man to ride the crane and ascend.” Qiu Changchun silently reflected on the words of the Three Officials: “Seven years of becoming a true one ought to flourish.” How could there be any principle of ascending today? Could it be that this is the attack of the inner yin demons within my mind, producing all these illusions to defeat my true Way? At this very moment of awakening, the two lads disappeared, and there was no white crane either — he was sitting alone upon half a meditation cushion. Outside the window the stars and moon shone together, and all sounds were still. This truly was a great many strange and extraordinary things springing up out of nothing; had it not been that his thought held fast, he would nearly have erred by a hair and lost by a thousand li! He reproached himself for having indulged in a moment’s whim to test Sai Mayi, and so brought down upon himself all these yin demons. If he did not refine away his yin air, how could he attain pure yang? He thought again that he must needs use a method of confounding the demons, so as to pare away the whole host of yin and leave them no crevice to exploit — this was the best course.

Thereupon he left Panxi and came to an earthen hill, where he saw at the slope’s foot a round stone weighing a hundred jin, and it was also a secluded spot. So he built a hut of thatch and sat in meditation within it. Whenever the yin demons manifested, he would come quickly, carry that round stone up the hill, move it to the middle of the slope, then let it fall again, and return to sit in stillness. As soon as visions arose, he would use the stone to confound them. Thus for three years the yin demons all withdrew, and his whole body became pure yang. All the various visions, entering his eye, were empty; his spiritual brightness grew ever clearer, and the heavenly mechanism responded of itself. He knew there was a certain matter at hand, but the heavenly mechanism could not be disclosed, so he must needs go and point it out. If he could cause that one to awaken, he might avoid this sinking, and would not fail the heavenly virtue that loves life, while opening below the gate of salvation. At that time he left the earthen hill to go and attend to this matter.

Now it is told that in the region of Kanlong there was a wealthy householder surnamed Wang, named Yun. His family was rich and prosperous, and everyone called him Wang the Great Household; he could rank as a money-lord. Dwelling beside the mountains and by the water, he naturally enjoyed the beauties of encircling hills and embracing streams, with a stream running outside his gate. Though this Wang Yun had so great an estate, he was by nature harsh and miserly, making a habit of using a large steelyard and a small measure, giving out light and taking in heavy. He did nothing but oppress the poor and bully the weak, seizing fields and taking land. The servants of his house, lending the fox’s authority to the tiger and the dog’s power to the man, swindled the village simpletons and debauched the women, doing every kind of wickedness. Relying on their master’s might they committed crimes that filled the sky, yet did not know it. Outside his gate there was a great stone, more than ten feet long and several feet high, with a large head and a small tail, like a lion — and so it was called the stone lion.

There were many people who worked for him outside; and whenever it came time to eat, the one who kept watch at the gate would stand upon the back of the stone lion and strike a clapper, which was heard on all four sides, and everyone would come back to eat — this was the usual practice. Not far off there was a hillside, and on it had been built a Guanyin temple, erected by the ancestors of Wang Yun. Land had been given and a resident monk installed. But when Wang Yun took charge, he drove the monk away and took back the land. Only he did not tear down the temple or smash the idol — this may be counted as a small remnant of good heart. Though the temple was left standing, it became a cold, neglected temple. Qiu Changchun, coming from the place of Baoji, lodged in this temple. Every day, hearing the clapper, he went to beg alms. He begged more than ten times, and no one paid him any attention. Not to speak of alms, he could not even obtain a mouthful of water. There was only a maidservant named Chunhua (Spring Flower), who, seeing him come several times, always with empty hands and leaving with empty hands, felt unable to bear it. She hid a few steamed buns, came out, and thrust them into Changchun’s sleeve, saying: “Old master, go quickly; this is no good place.” After another two days, Qiu Changchun came to beg alms and happened to meet Wang Yun standing at the gate. Changchun had originally come to convert him; now seeing him standing before the gate, he spoke four lines to move him:
For greed of fame and profit one will not turn back; when impermanence comes in a day, all things end.
Though one possess gold and silver, he cannot carry them away; in vain do two eyes leave long-streaming tears.

Changchun had no sooner finished speaking than Wang Yun flew into a rage: “You wild Daoist, do not go on talking nonsense here! All my life I have been a man who does not believe in the Buddha’s Dharma. Leave quickly, lest you suffer humiliation.” Changchun said: “This poor Daoist has come especially to beg alms at your honored house; may the master freely bestow a little charity.” Wang Yun saw that outside the gate there was a basket for collecting horse dung, filled with horse dung, and beside it a shovel for picking up dung. He took up the shovel, scooped out a shovel of horse dung, and going before Changchun said: “You ask me to bestow charity — how about my bestowing this thing upon you?” Changchun was just about to test his heart; seeing him act thus, and fearing it might be mere play, he thrust his gourd ladle forward, and he thereupon poured a shovel of horse dung into it. Qiu Changchun said: “Of what use is this horse dung to me?” Wang Yun said: “This dung is all gathered by the laborers I have hired; giving it to you today also counts as my charity.”

Hearing this, Changchun said: “Well done! Well done!” Thereupon Wang Yun and all his servants laughed. The whole household, great and small, on hearing these words, all burst out laughing; only Chunhua was uneasy at heart. One day, seeing that the servants had all gone up the slope to work, she hid a few steamed buns in her sleeve and came out. It happened that Changchun was standing outside the gate, and she was about to give him the steamed buns. Changchun said: “I have not come to beg alms. I have one important sentence to tell you; remember it firmly. When you see the stone lion before the gate with red eyes, you may go up to the Guanyin temple on the hill and hide for a while, and then you will be safe from harm.” Having said this, he drifted away, and at once disappeared.

Chunhua kept these words in her heart, and every day came out to look at the stone lion twice. Thus for several months, until a herdboy who watched the cattle made out her situation and asked: “Sister Chunhua, why do you come out every day to look at this stone lion?” Chunhua told him: “The old master who came begging alms that day told me to come at once to the Guanyin temple to hide for a while when the stone lion’s eyes turned red, so as to escape a great calamity.” Hearing this, the herdboy thought it very strange. Wanting to tease her, he secretly found a piece of red earth. In the afternoon, driving the cattle home, he climbed up onto the stone lion and smeared two round circles on its face with the red earth, making them look like a pair of eyes. When he had finished, he came down and slipped aside, to see what she would do.

At that time the sky was about to turn to evening. Chunhua, within, suddenly felt her heart leap and her eyes start, and she could neither walk nor sit in peace. Thinking in her heart, “Can it be that the stone lion’s eyes have turned red?” she hurried out to look, not caring that her master might scold her. Coming out, she indeed saw the stone lion with both eyes bright red. Greatly alarmed, she ran to the Guanyin temple. The herdboy, seeing her run up to the temple, also followed behind. Just as he was about to reach the temple and question her, suddenly there burst a great thunderclap that shook the mountains and moved the earth. Before long a wild wind rose on all sides, black clouds filled the sky, and in an instant a torrential rain poured down, as if a ladle were being emptied and a pail overturned. It rained straight on until the middle of the night before the rain stopped. Chunhua and the herdboy lay hidden under the incense table, hearing crash after crash of sound, like a thousand men beating drums, with the momentum of ten thousand horses racing. Only at daybreak did they dare come out to look. Indeed, before looking it was one thing; after looking they were frightened out of their wits! The fact was that this estate of Wang Yun, no one knew at what time last night, had been passed through by a dragon, which, seeing the house built so handsomely, had borrowed it for its Crystal Palace. Only the stone lion was unwilling to go, and lay fallen in the middle of the river.

Now Chunhua, seeing that Wang Yun’s whole family had been carried off by the flood, could not help being sad and shedding tears. Before long she had stirred up the people near and far, great and small, male and female, who all came to look. Everyone said that Heaven had eyes, and that retribution was without error. Seeing Chunhua weeping, they asked: “Your master’s whole family has been destroyed; how did you escape with your life?” Chunhua then told them all of the words the Daoist had instructed. The villagers discussed the matter, all saying that Wang Yun was full of wickedness to the brim, and Heaven had sent a flood. That Daoist must surely have been a spirit, who came to point the way to him; but he would not turn his heart, and so was carried off by the water. Though you are a maidservant, you have a bit of good root, and so were saved, and you also brought the herdboy along with you, so that he did not die. It seems that a person born between heaven and earth should always do some good deeds, so that when a great calamity comes there may be a savior.

They asked Chunhua again: “What will you do hereafter?” Chunhua said: “This temple was built by the old master in former years, and the lands all about have already been given to the temple. Now I shall cultivate here in this temple, wearing my hair and practicing, and I no longer yearn for that gorgeous, glittering world or the bright beauty of the red dust.” The people said: “That is very good. We will gather a little traveling money for you to get by for the time being, and after the autumn harvest you will not lack food or use.” Having said this, they each gathered some money and grain and gave them to Chunhua, and also found an old woman to keep her company. Chunhua thanked them all, and from then on practiced with a single, undivided heart. After several years, the True Man Qiu was resting quietly in the Longmen cave. Knowing that she truly sought the Way, he came and converted her. She then bowed to the True Man as her teacher, and later also attained the right fruit.

It is further told that after Qiu Changchun had instructed Chunhua, he entered the mountains of Longzhou. He saw a stone cliff, and in the cliff there was a cave — the place where, in the time between the end of Qin and the beginning of Han, Mr. Lou Jing determined the sun and moon. Below it was a stream, and the overhanging rock cliff faced the stream. The water curved and turned; seen from afar, the cliff seemed to straddle the stream, and the cave was like a gate. People of the time set store by success in the examinations, and seeing this mountain cave like a gate, they named it Dragon Gate (Longmen), taking the meaning of a carp leaping over the dragon gate. Changchun, arriving here, at last understood the words of Master Chongyang, “the dragon flies over the gate,” and knew they were fulfilled in this place. So by the gate of the cave he nourished his nature and cultivated his truth.

Before two years had passed, Longzhou suffered a drought. The governor of Longzhou led the people of the commandery in prayer, but the rain did not fall. Seeing the seedlings withered and scorched, and the myriad people in grief and toil, Qiu Changchun went to the commandery seat, saying of himself that he could pray for three days of sweet rain to save the multitudes. The prefectural officials were greatly pleased and reverently invited him to ascend the altar. Qiu Changchun then neatened his robe and cap, prostrated himself at the altar and court, and with a single thought of sincerity reached the Emperor on high. Indeed a drenching rain fell, continuing for three days and three nights; the fields and crops were abundant, and the myriad people were at peace.

The next year, the region of Beizhi (the area directly under the capital) suffered a great heavenly drought, with long dryness and no rain. The Son of Heaven led the hundred officials in prayer, but still the rain did not fall. Emperor Shun of the Yuan issued an edict, hanging up a placard to recruit men of the Way, of pure and lofty conduct, to pray for rain. Whoever could obtain rain would be given high office and rank to repay his labor. The imperial placard was hung, and all the provinces learned of it. The governor of Longzhou recommended one man who could obtain rain. But who was this man? Look at the passage below.
In years past beset by famine, today I move the emperor.

blocks.text: 26. Praying for Sweet Rain to Turn Heaven and Change the Sun; Working a Wondrous Art to Exchange the Phoenix and Steal the Dragon

inline.s: A single sincerity can move Heaven, and turn an evil year into a year of plenty;
Do not say the Yuan ruler loves the people so deeply; it is still that the True Man’s Way is wondrous and profound.

The story goes that Emperor Shun of the Yuan hung the imperial placard, seeking out a man of pure and lofty practice in the Way to pray for rain. The governor of Longzhou sent a memorial to the capital, stating: “The lofty scholar of the Way, Qiu Changchun, of Longmen in Longzhou, is pure and noble in virtue. Last year Longzhou suffered a drought; thanks to this man’s power, sweet rain was obtained, saving the multitudes. Now the emperor wishes to obtain rain to relieve the people’s distress, and no one but this man can do it. Since saving the people is a matter of utmost urgency, I submit this for the imperial notice.” Emperor Shun of the Yuan, having read the memorial, was delighted at heart, and immediately ordered the grand physician Hali Tuotuo to go and engage Changchun. Before long he arrived at Longmen, presented jade and silk, and declared the emperor’s will. Changchun joyfully accepted the summons and went with the physician to Beijing. The next day he had audience with the Yuan ruler, who honored him with the courtesy of a teacher, seating him above the nine ministers, and entrusted him with the task of praying for rain.

Changchun submitted: “The emperor’s heart is anxious for the people; how would your minister dare not to exert a trifling effort? But two altars must be erected on high, and the emperor must personally burn incense and worship. Your minister will then pray to the Emperor on high, and set a limit of three days for the rain.” The Yuan ruler was greatly pleased, and immediately ordered the responsible authorities to manage the matter, and also sent a eunuch to escort Changchun to the Jixian Hall to take up residence.

At the morning audience the next day, the responsible authorities memorialized that the rain altar had been erected, awaiting the master to ascend it. The Yuan ruler then summoned Changchun to go with him to the altar. The Son of Heaven personally burned incense and, when the worship was finished, returned with his carriage to the palace. Changchun prostrated himself before the rain altar and prayed in earnest. On the third day, at the hour of noon (one in the afternoon), the red sun hung in the sky like a wheel of fire, scorching the ground into dust and making every person stream with sweat. Changchun dipped a willow branch in pure water and sprinkled it toward the red sun. Before long a wisp of black air grew beside the sun, and in an instant (
shū

, suddenly) turned into cloud, veiling the red sun. In a moment the sky grew dark and the earth dim, and a great rain fell in torrents, continuing for several days, turning dryness into flourishing and withered things back to spring. The people rejoiced, and all living things relied on it. Emperor Shun of the Yuan was greatly pleased, conferred upon Changchun the title of Hongdao True Man, and kept him in the capital, treating him with the courtesy due to a most honored guest.

One day, the Yuan ruler summoned the True Man within, and they strolled to the imperial garden. In this garden there were ever-green grass and unfading flowers, with strange rocks and wondrous trees beyond description. The Yuan ruler and the True Man sat together on a rock, discussing the Way and the mystery. Five-colored auspicious clouds spread over the sky, like a canopy.

When they came to the subtle and most refined points, the Yuan ruler sighed: “Were I not he who has inherited the great line, I would wish to wander with Master Chisongzi. Once I have a successor, I shall bow to the True Man as my teacher and enter the mountains to cultivate.” The True Man Qiu said: “Let the sovereign not worry; the empress has already conceived the dragon fetus, and before long shall bear the heir apparent.” The Yuan ruler thought to himself: “The True Man is indeed a spirit, for he knows of the pregnancy in the inner palace,” and so he answered casually: “The empress is indeed with child, but does one know whether it is a boy or a girl?” The True Man Qiu said: “Your minister has calculated it to be a boy, and it is beyond all doubt.” The Yuan ruler said: “If it turns out as my teacher says, it shall be my fortune.” The True Man withdrew. Emperor Shun of the Yuan returned to the palace and said to the empress: “The True Man Qiu has calculated that you, my consort, are with child of the dragon fetus; one knows not whether it is certain.” The empress replied: “How could he calculate so precisely? Why not summon the national preceptor to the hall, and have him calculate together with the True Man; if the two agree, then it may be held certain.” The Yuan ruler was delighted, and the next day summoned the White Cloud meditation master of the White Cloud temple to the hall, to calculate together with the True Man Qiu: whether the empress’s pregnancy was a boy or a girl.

The White Cloud meditation master counted on his fingers and submitted: “According to your minister’s calculation, the empress carries the phoenix fetus, and shall surely bear a princess.” The Yuan ruler asked the True Man Qiu again, and the True Man submitted: “Your minister made it clear to the sovereign yesterday that the empress carries the dragon fetus and must bear the heir apparent; why trouble to ask again?” The White Cloud meditation master laughed: “Since you have gained insight into the mystery, you must surely understand the art of numbers. Calculate it once more.” The True Man Qiu said: “Whether calculated or not, it is always the dragon fetus, and must be a male.” The meditation master said angrily: “The numbers I calculate are without omission; how dare you speak wildly and disturb the sage virtue!” The True Man Qiu said: “The art of numbers is not equal to the principle of Heaven; hidden virtue has the power to turn back Heaven, and good deeds have the merit to frustrate fate. Now the sovereign has personally prayed for rain, saving the multitudes, and even the insects, herbs, and trees have shared in his grace — this is a great hidden virtue. Perhaps it has moved Heaven to turn a girl into a boy, and transform a phoenix into a dragon; who can say for certain?” The White Cloud meditation master said: “I took you for a man of the Way, but in truth you are only ordinary. The pregnancy came first and the rain-praying came after; how could there be a completed fetus that is afterward altered?” The True Man Qiu said: “I have already determined it; why must I argue forcibly?” The White Cloud meditation master said: “Dare you make a wager with me?” The True Man Qiu said: “A wager is a wager; what is there I dare not?” The White Cloud meditation master said: “If it is a dragon fetus, I will stake the White Cloud temple against you.” The True Man Qiu said: “If it is a phoenix fetus, I am willing to stake my head.” The meditation master laughed: “Do not regret it afterward.” The True Man said: “A single word is the standard; what regret could there be?” The meditation master said: “Words alone are no proof; you must draw up a written agreement for evidence.”

The True Man Qiu then asked for paper and brush before the imperial presence, and before the dragon desk wrote out an agreement: “Qiu Changchun, who stakes his head upon this wager, now wagers with the White Cloud meditation master. If the principal mother of the inner palace bears a phoenix, Qiu Changchun loses, and is willing to yield up the head upon his neck, without any objection.” The White Cloud meditation master also took up his brush and wrote before the imperial presence: “He who stakes the White Cloud temple, the White Cloud monk, now wagers with Qiu Changchun. If the principal mother of the inner palace bears a dragon, the White Cloud monk loses, and is willing to stake the White Cloud temple against Qiu Changchun, without any objection for all time.” When written, the two affixed their signatures. They exchanged, each read the other’s over once, and then presented them to the imperial desk. Emperor Shun of the Yuan cast his eyes over them and kept them himself, to await the empress’s delivery, and then the outcome would be known. That day the court was dismissed, and each returned to his place.

Now the White Cloud meditation master, returning to the White Cloud temple, reflected that Qiu Changchun had been so resolute and decisive — could it be that the empress was indeed carrying a dragon fetus, and that he had miscalculated? Unable to rest easy, he pushed his reckoning of the numbers again, and found no error, and so rejoiced inwardly. He said to himself: “Qiu Changchun, you cannot blame me. You have brought this calamity on yourself and thrown away your own life, all in vain for having cultivated the Way.” It is further told that the True Man Qiu, returning to the Jixian Hall, reckoned the day of the empress’s delivery, and sent up a spirit talisman, borrowing from within the palace of the ninth heaven’s Mysterious Maiden a spirit maiden named Yuzhen the Fairy, who could transform endlessly and whose spiritual powers were vast. This fairy, by command of the ninth heaven’s Holy Mother, came to await the True Man Qiu’s direction. The True Man Qiu respectfully said to the fairy: “Tonight, at the hour of the Ox, the princess of the Prince Ning’s residence shall bear a child. You shall change a gourd into a female baby, exchange it for his boy, and carry the boy to the golden throne hall. After I have exchanged the phoenix, you will take the phoenix and exchange back the gourd.” The spirit maiden received the command and went to carry it out.

That night, at the hour of the Rat, the empress gave birth to a girl, which indeed bore out the white cloud meditation master’s word of a phoenix fetus; the palace attendants reported it to the Yuan ruler. Emperor Shun of the Yuan greatly admired the meditation master’s calculation as accurate, and yet was anxious that the True Man’s life could hardly be spared, and that he must devise some means to save him — this was the proper course for a ruler. So he set the morning court; the officials all knew the empress had borne a princess, and came at once to offer congratulations. The White Cloud meditation master also came to congratulate, submitting: “Your minister has heard that the empress has borne the heir apparent, continuing the line of the holy court, and your minister is beyond measure delighted. I only wish our sovereign ten thousand years, and the crown prince a thousand autumns.” Emperor Shun of the Yuan sighed: “My fate should be to lack a successor, and that is not enough to regret; but the True Man Qiu miscalculated yin and yang, and so the loss is due. Mindful of his merit in praying for rain, I wish to save him; I am willing to give one hundred thousand of the imperial treasury to make good the White Cloud temple, in order to redeem the True Man’s head.” While the Yuan ruler was speaking, the White Cloud meditation master was still hesitating, when the yellow-gate official announced that the True Man Qiu had come to court. The Yuan ruler ordered him admitted at once. When the True Man Qiu had finished his courtesies, he also congratulated the Yuan ruler: “The empress has produced the stored dragon; your minister has therefore come to offer congratulations.” The Yuan ruler said: “The True Man is mistaken; the empress has borne a daughter.” The True Man Qiu said: “Your minister’s calculation is beyond all doubt; if it is indeed a daughter, I beg that she be brought out for your minister to see, and then your minister will die content.”

The Yuan ruler had originally wished to shield and save him; now seeing him so stiffly upright, he could not but be displeased. So he ordered the palace maid to go within and bring out the female infant. By this time it had reached the hour of dawn, and the spirit maiden had already transformed a gourd into a female infant, exchanged it for the boy, and hidden her spirit light; she had waited long in the golden throne hall. When the palace maid brought out the female infant and returned before the imperial presence, the Yuan ruler had the maid hand it to the True Man to examine. Qiu Changchun took it in both hands, and with a glance of his robe-sleeve, the spirit maiden had already exchanged the dragon for the phoenix, changing a boy for the female infant, and delivered the boy to the prince’s residence. The officials were all of mortal eyes and fleshly frames — how could they see it? The White Cloud meditation master had a bit of wisdom but no spiritual power, so how could he know? At once the True Man Qiu, having used this art of stealing the dragon and exchanging the phoenix, held the boy in both hands and asked the whole assembly of officials to look, to see whether it was male or female. Having looked, the officials all cried out: “Long live the crown prince!” The White Cloud meditation master’s face lost its color in rage. He came over, took the child in his hands, and looked — clearly it was a boy, and not a female infant at all! His face flushed red all over, and he could only congratulate the Yuan ruler too: “It is indeed the stored dragon of the later court.” Having said this, he presented the boy. The Yuan ruler, seeing it, was greatly astonished at the affair, and immediately changed his words: “I heard the palace attendants report, and had not personally seen the child, and so took it to be a female infant; this is the error of the inner palace.” He then ordered the imperial kitchen to spread a banquet for three days, and proclaimed a great amnesty through the realm. The Yuan ruler went out of the hall, and the civil and military officials dispersed. The True Man Qiu asked the White Cloud meditation master: “How does my master direct?” The White Cloud meditation master said: “A single word once spoken cannot be overtaken by four horses. Tomorrow I shall hand over the temple to you; you move in, and I move out, and all matters are settled. What further direction is there?” Having said this, each returned to his own temple.

The True Man Qiu had no sooner returned to the hall when the spirit maiden came to return the gourd, and thereupon ascended to the ninth heaven. This is not to be narrated. It is further told that the White Cloud meditation master, returning to the White Cloud temple, would not accept it. He pushed his reckoning of the numbers again, and still could not work it out. Truly, “Being one move higher, it is hard to win the game; being three parts weaker in skill, it is always a loss.” Watching with his own eyes the ground he must give up, he could not but sigh! There was an attendant at his side who said to the meditation master: “Qiu Changchun, alone as he is, how can he occupy so great a temple? Let us have one man match one man, one exchange for another. If we cannot match them all, nor exchange them all, we shall still remain here and slowly work out a plan.” Hearing this, the meditation master was delighted. The next day the True Man Qiu arrived, and the White Cloud meditation master said: “Many monks, a wide dwelling; a broad temple, a crowded throng. For every one you bring, I will move out one monk. One exchanges for one, one man matches one man. If they cannot all be exchanged, then we shall not all leave, so that the monks may dwell and the Daoists may dwell.” The True Man Qiu said: “Excellent! This is precisely what I would wish. I shall go before the mountain gate and call them in.” Having said this, he walked outside the mountain gate, took the whisk from his sleeve, pulled out some of the whisk’s palm-fiber strands, and tossed them into the sky. What did this come to? Look at the next chapter for the outcome.
Do not say that today my human power is small; know that beside me there is much of the profound and mysterious.

blocks.text: 27. Earnestly Admonishing Us All; Discussing Cultivation as Done Layer by Layer

inline.s: Flowers fall and flowers bloom, and another year passes; in human life, how often does one see the moon always full?
Break open the fame and profit that are a lock without a bar; where the fierce fire blazes, well may one plant the lotus.

The story goes that the True Man Qiu walked out the mountain gate and drew the whisk from his sleeve. Secretly snapping off some of the palm-fiber strands from the whisk, he blew upon them a breath of true breath and tossed them into the sky; they were scattered by the wind, and no one knew where they fell. In an instant a host of Daoists came, following the True Man Qiu in, and exchanged all the monks of the temple. The White Cloud meditation master took up residence in the Jixian Hall where the True Man Qiu had dwelt, and these monks scattered among the various temples to shelter themselves. Why did the True Man Qiu insist on this White Cloud temple? Because in the region of Beijing the kingly air was at its height, and he knew it was a place fit for a long-lasting capital, and wished to take advantage of this flourishing land to open an altar and carry on the teaching. In the second place, the White Cloud meditation master was destined to flourish in the south, and to unfold the teaching throughout the region of the three rivers. Had he long remained in the capital keeping this White Cloud temple, he could never unfold it. Therefore he took the temple, so as to let him go south and widely save sentient beings. Hence the heavenly and earthly true men each have their proper place: one may be benefited by this and not by that, another by that and not by this. When the noble one cultivates his truth, he must take a place in accordance with, and responding to, that which is mutually life-giving; as for that which is mutually overcoming and mutually obstructive, he avoids it. This is what is called obtaining the advantage of the land.

Tarrying no longer with idle talk, it is told that the True Man Qiu gathered fellow Daoists in the White Cloud temple, and within a month several tens of fellow practitioners had come. For the handling of affairs each was assigned a duty, and in no time it grew lively. The True Man Qiu, seeing that the fellow practitioners were unequal in wisdom and dullness, could not but give them an instruction.
The True Man Qiu said to the assembly of friends:

What is called leaving the home life is to leave the dust and depart from the world. One must first have a mind that has seen through the vulgar world and a heart that dwells in seclusion seeking the Way; only then can it be called leaving home with a true heart. If one leaves home in a momentary wild hope of becoming an immortal, or out of anger, or out of greed for ease and leisure, then one uses the Way as a pretext and is in truth only settling one’s own body. Hence a fierce, resolute heart is easily roused, but a heart that endures long is hard to obtain. Because the Way is treated as optional — as something that may or may not be — one in the end loses the profound mystery. Again there are those who, having lost the support of their elders in childhood and being alone in old age, leave home; they only borrow our gate to shelter their body — what is there for them to see through?

In a word, since they have come, let them be at ease. Whether they see through it or not, if they come to the land of the Three Jewels, they are all people of affinity. Those who enter my gate are not poor, and those who leave my gate are not rich. Since they have entered my gate, they should embody my heart. The highest practice the mystery and sit in meditation; the middle recite scriptures and honor the precepts; the lowest do hard work and labor. Even so can the work of one who has left home be accomplished.

What others cannot do, I will strive to be able to do. What others cannot bear, I will make my heart bear. To be able is to be able to cut off passion and desire; to bear is to be able to bear hunger and cold. Thus one surpasses others. One should make the heart empty and void, not letting in the least obstruction, nor stirring up any speck of partiality. Not only is there no other person, but further no self; and since what I call ‘self’ does not exist, from where could the demons arise? Only by seeking the Way within this emptiness and nothingness does the skill come of itself. If one does his work upon contrivance, he instead loses the true Way. In all things, measure your strength and act accordingly, neither over nor under. Those who know the greater accomplish the greater, and those who know the smaller accomplish the smaller. Keeping to the line and the rule, following the measure and the pattern — though one may not become an immortal or a Buddha, one will not fail to be a good man! Thus one will not have left home in vain.

If one only knows that coiling the topknot is the Way, and that shaving the head makes a monk, while the five aggregates are not emptied and the four marks are not forgotten — outwardly a proper robe and cap, inwardly almost a beast of the fields; the mind of fame and profit not yet thin, the heart of right and wrong ever present; extravagance in one’s thoughts, only fearing that one’s clothes and food are not equal to others’; hope held in luck, always wishing that what one does and leaves undone all goes as one wishes — such a person, though he says he has left home, has in fact not left home; and though he is called one of the Way, is not in the Way at all. Looked at in this light, he would be better off returning to the lay life and to his home, exchanging bitterness for delight. Why linger long in the gate of the mystery, using the Way as a livelihood, and commit infinite sin? Since in this life he cannot be lifted up, in the life to come he will yet sink in the sea of suffering. Thus the fruit of blessing of this life is not obtained, while the sin of the life to come is planted early — one should reflect upon this!”

Just as the True Man Qiu was delivering his words, there came more than ten men beyond the mountain gate, all tall and stalwart. Who were these men? They were the several good fellows who had rescued the True Man on Mount Qinling in former years — Zhao Bi, Wang Neng, Zhu Jiu, and the rest — together with a band of brothers, coming to this White Cloud temple. The fact was that they had saved the True Man Qiu’s life on Mount Qinling years before, and had been awakened by a few words on karmic retribution, cause, and fruit. Each turned from evil to the right, and took up a business of general merchandise, traveling through the lands of Youyan (the region of Yan and You). They could make a living, and so passed more than ten years.

Zhao Bi, Li Xiong, and Zhang Jian were all old by now, and only Wang Neng and Zhu Jiu had not yet grown beards. They had heard people say that in the White Cloud temple there was a Great True Man Qiu, a man of the Way who had prayed for sweet rain the previous year and saved the multitudes, and who afterward had calculated that the imperial consort would bear a crown prince, made a wager with the White Cloud meditation master, and won an entire White Cloud temple in his hands. Now he was widely recruiting men who studied the Way and practiced, expounding the scriptures and preaching the Dharma there. Hearing these words, they were all delighted. Zhao Bi said: “In those years on Mount Qinling we saved that old master, whose placard bore the line, ‘Qiu of such-and-such has set forth to practice.’ Can it be that he has now attained the Way? Why not go together to the White Cloud temple and have a look.” Zhang Jian said: “We often travel about seeking men of the Way; perhaps today we may fulfill our wish.” Zhu Jiu said: “So long as he has the Way and has virtue, let us bow to him as our teacher and leave home.” Zhao Bi said: “The words of brother Zhu are very refreshing.”
